name: Looksmax.org / forum participation

lead: Looksmax.org is described as one of the main hubs of looksmaxxing, alongside forum.looksmaxxing.com. Members post photos for feedback, ask for ratings and share guides, using the replies as a map for what to improve in their face and body.

The chain is simple: post photos, get a current and 'potential' PSL score from peers, read the shared guides, then apply tips on skin, grooming, fitness or procedures. The feedback comes from peers on a self-devised rating scale, and the guides' methods range from studied to anecdotal.

paras: Members typically post front and side photos, discuss softmaxxing (non-invasive changes) and hardmaxxing (surgery, steroids), and use shared vocabulary such as canthal tilt and hunter eyes. Many post progress photos over months to track changes. Anonymity is common.

Commentators and researchers link the subculture to body dysmorphia, depression and anxiety, promotion of dangerous methods, blackpill determinism and radicalisation. Critics also call the PSL scale unscientific and biased against non-white men. Members often gatekeep against casual 'normies'.

angle.text: Members post progress photos, request ratings and swap guides, using the feedback and shared methods as a map for improving face and body. The ratings come from peers on a self-devised scale, and the guides' methods vary from studied to anecdotal.

lead: Looksmax.org is an online forum devoted to improving male appearance, and is described as one of the main hubs of looksmaxxing alongside forum.looksmaxxing.com.[1] Members use it to get feedback on how they look and to find guides on what to change: they post photos for rating threads, track progress photos over months, and read or write guides covering skincare, grooming, hair, fitness, posture and, for some, surgery and medical treatments.[2][1]

Looksmaxxing took shape on message boards in the 2010s. Wikipedia names PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, now defunct, as the 'PSL forums' that devised the PSL rating scale of facial attractiveness, and notes that male content creators popularized the practice on TikTok in the early 2020s.[2] Looksmax.org itself is a later forum; Female-oriented guides reportedly appeared on it in 2024 and 2025.[1]

The forum has published its own member surveys. Its 2025 survey, reporting on respondents with fewer than 1,000 posts (1,593 responses), found about 62 percent under 18 and roughly 90 percent under 21, with about 99.5 percent identifying as male.[3] Commentators and researchers have also raised concerns about the wider subculture, which are covered below.
infobox: Guides, PSL rating threads, progress photos

paras: Looksmaxxing took shape on incel-linked boards in the mid-2010s.[2][1] After Reddit banned r/incels in 2017, activity moved to independent forums, often on.is domains, and from around 2020 to TikTok, where it reached non-incel audiences.[1] Wikipedia describes early TikTok videos as often presenting looksmaxxing as self-improvement with self-deprecating humor, with black pill ideology becoming more associated with it in mainstream discourse by the mid-2020s.[2]

Looksmax.org has run its own TikTok account, an announcement that drew mixed reactions from members in a forum thread, some of whom said the move would make the forum more mainstream.[4] Members have also compared the forum with its Discord server, with some describing the Discord as rating-focused.[5]

Members post progress photos and request ratings on current and potential PSL, sometimes using wet-hair photos to reduce styling effects.[1] Ratings are competitive and quantify perceived genetic potential.[1] Anonymity is common, and members gatekeep against casual 'normies'.[1] Core vocabulary includes softmaxxing (non-invasive changes such as skincare, grooming and fitness), hardmaxxing (surgery, drugs and other invasive measures), blackpill, canthal tilt, hunter eyes, mewing and bonesmashing.[2][1]

The forum's 2025 survey summary, posted by its administrators, reported that most respondents were very young and almost entirely male, with about 42 percent between 170 and 179 cm tall and about 39 percent between 180 and 189 cm, and North America the largest region.[3] Earlier annual survey threads exist for 2024, and the forum has marked anniversaries with community events.[6][7]

Commentators describe the practice as judgemental and link it to body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation, and researchers say it promotes hegemonic masculinity.[2] Wikipedia also reports that researchers say TikTok algorithms can draw young men toward incel views, that doctors have criticized mewing and bonesmashing as misinformation, and that some men report benefits such as improved confidence or relationships.[2]

Grokipedia lists controversies including blackpill determinism, misogynistic slang, promotion of unproven methods such as bonesmashing and unregulated overseas surgery with reported complications, criticism of PSL as unscientific, and research linking the subculture to radicalisation.[1]
No studies found. Published research on online health and appearance forums in general, such as analyses of weight-loss subreddits and drug-use forums, concerns other communities.[8]

timeline.event: Looksmaxxing forms on incel-linked boards such as Lookism.net and Sluthate.[2][1]
Reddit bans r/incels, pushing activity to independent forums.[1]
Looksmax.org publishes a community survey; female-oriented guides reportedly begin appearing around this time.[1][6]
Looksmax.org publishes another survey of its members.[3]
